attempts.user_message:
Please review the following manuscript I wrote.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b07/review-experiment-6jxq6vrv/call-b895d04af7eb42c6af2baa0ece7997f4/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'ls -la && ls -l manuscript.pdf && command -v pdftotext && command -v pdftoppm && command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'
import sys, importlib.util, shutil
print(sys.executable)
for name in ['pypdf','pdfplumber','fitz','PIL','pypdfium2']:
 print(name, bool(importlib.util.find_spec(name)))
for name in ['pdftotext','pdftoppm','pdfinfo','gs']:
 print(name, shutil.which(name))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:',len(r.pages))
print('Metadata:',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
 texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))
PY"

/bin/bash -c "gs -q -dSAFER -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -sDEVICE=png16m -r250 -dFirstPage=2 -dLastPage=2 -sOutputFile=tmp/pdfs/figure1-page.png manuscript.pdf && python3 - <<'PY'
from PIL import Image
im=Image.open('tmp/pdfs/figure1-page.png')
im.crop((170,200,1960,900)).save('tmp/pdfs/figure1.png')
PY"

/bin/bash -c "gs -q -dSAFER -dBATCH -dNOPAUSE -sDEVICE=png16m -r250 -dFirstPage=6 -dLastPage=6 -sOutputFile=tmp/pdfs/figure3-page.png manuscript.pdf && python3 - <<'PY'
from PIL import Image
im=Image.open('tmp/pdfs/figure3-page.png')
im.crop((170,220,1960,990)).save('tmp/pdfs/figure3.png')
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human response times under changing external stimuli. Combining task-derived neural features with a controllable evidence-accumulation process is a well-motivated approach, and Figure 1 clearly communicates the overall architecture.

The two-day study provides repeated behavioral measurements across four stimulus conditions. Evaluating general, group, individual, and leave-one-participant-out settings is useful; the latter provides stronger evidence of generalization than shuffled trial splits alone.

The results provide preliminary evidence of practical value. Hybrid DRL achieves lower aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in all four settings, including 0.2905 versus 0.3037 under leave-one-participant-out evaluation. The reported training times of 4.42 versus 38.30 minutes also suggest a potential computational benefit.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are unavailable in the supplied manuscript. The referenced appendices S2–S6 are absent, leaving the RL algorithm and reward, evidence-update equations, diffusion noise, mapping from SVM predictions to DDM parameters, important hyperparameters, and adaptive stimulus rule insufficiently specified. Promised future code availability does not resolve these gaps, which prevent reproduction and assessment of the central method.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of incorporating DDM. Pure DRL simultaneously removes DDM and replaces frame-level sequential decisions with a single trial-level action. Consequently, improvements could arise from temporal processing or the changed optimization problem. Comparisons with a matched sequential predictor, supervised response-time residual regression, and a fitted stimulus-dependent DDM are needed to establish the proposed combination's contribution.

The claimed cognitive interpretation exceeds the evidence. Observed response times do not uniquely identify within-trial evidence trajectories: multiple action sequences can produce the same threshold-crossing time. Agreement with aggregate behavioral trends therefore does not validate the inferred mechanism. Substantial nonzero 'time-pressure effect' trajectories also appear in the no-pressure condition (Figure 3p), suggesting that the controller can absorb baseline prediction error. Recovery experiments or predictions under independently varied stimulus schedules would provide more convincing validation.

The evaluation protocol needs clarification. It is unclear which no-pressure observations train the baseline SVMs and whether all human-data-dependent fitting, normalization, and tuning exclude held-out participants in each outer split. This leaves potential information leakage unresolved rather than demonstrated. Shuffled trial evaluations also do not establish forecasting performance on later trials or unfamiliar stimulus schedules.

The predictive gains over Pure DRL are modest, and their reliability is not quantified. For example, general-level MAPE changes from 0.3034 to 0.2999. Confidence intervals, paired participant-level comparisons, and reported variability across random seeds are needed to judge these differences. The training-efficiency claim similarly lacks a clearly specified convergence criterion and uncertainty.

The behavioral conclusions require more caution. Only 36 participants remain after exclusions, with seven in the random condition, and the criteria for removing three 'extreme outliers' are unspecified. Normalization against the first formal block uses a baseline already exposed to the assigned intervention and does not eliminate individual differences. The reported random-versus-none difference supports a limited comparison, not a demonstrated advantage over every other condition; nonsignificant accuracy differences likewise do not establish equivalence.

The distinction from prior work is insufficiently developed. The paper cites existing RL–DDM integration, including Pedersen et al. (2017), but offers limited technical comparison. The suggestion that DDM supports posterior estimation rather than prediction is not a sound general distinction. Novelty should be established around the specific learned stimulus-dependent modulation and its demonstrated benefits.
